summary.text: 了 is traditionally explained as a pictograph related to 子, described in the received account as 子 without arms. Later interpretations connect its form with crossed or entangled legs. The character is also used for “finish” and Mandarin aspect and change-of-state particles; the picture’s old name and any sound link to “finish” are unverified.

formation.text: The received pictographic account describes 了 as 子 without arms. Later commentary instead interprets the form as crossed or entangled legs. These are competing readings of the graph; neither confirms what an early inscription depicted.

history.text: The received account relates the graph to 子, while later commentary interprets it through crossed or entangled legs. No securely dated earliest form or sequence of graphic changes is established in the cited accounts.

uncertainties.text: The graph may have been reused to write the word “finish” because the old name for the depicted form and “finish” sounded alike or similarly. The old name and sound match are unverified; a semantic path from entanglement through tying to completion has also been proposed, but lacks dated intermediate examples.

Historical accounts describe development of the particles across the Tang–Song period, but the cited summaries do not provide dated primary examples. A possible interaction between sentence-final 了 and 也 in some dialects remains tentative.

senses.text: The received entry glosses 了 with 尦; later commentary interprets this as legs crossing or becoming entangled. This interpretation does not directly confirm what an early inscription depicted.

Historical dictionary citations include “finish; be completed.” A Tang poem uses 未了 for “not ended” or “not finished.” The earliest attestation and the connection between this meaning and the pictorial interpretations remain unresolved.

senses.text: Accounts describe the completed-action marker developing from the verb “finish,” with resultative uses between the verb and aspect marking.

senses.text: Accounts describe the sentence-final change-of-state use as a later development from the perfective particle. Its detailed path remains uncertain, including a proposed interaction with 也 in some dialects.

developments.text: Accounts describe the completed-action marker developing from the verb “finish,” with resultative uses along the way.
Accounts describe the sentence-final change-of-state use developing from the perfective use. A possible interaction with 也 is proposed for some dialects, but the details remain unresolved.

limitations.text: The connection between “finish” and the graph is unresolved: proposed accounts invoke sound-based reuse or a semantic path from the entangled-legs interpretation. No early spelling or dated intermediate examples settle the question.
Later dictionary citations report both “understand clearly” and “finish,” but do not establish their relative chronology or a semantic connection.

overview.text: In Mandarin, 了 commonly marks a completed action or a change of state. One proposal says the graph was reused for “finish” because its old name sounded like that word, but the old name and sound match are unverified.
